title: How to count every fish in a lake with two catches
description:
You can't drain a lake to count its fish, so you fish twice. Catch 200, tag them and let them go; a few days later catch 200 again. If 20 of them are tagged, that's 1 in 10, so your 200 tagged fish are a tenth of the lake: about 2,000 fish. In 200,000 simulated lakes, 9 estimates in 10 land between 1,500 and 2,900; catching 500 each trip narrows it to 1,800-2,300. It only works if tagged fish are as easy to catch as the rest. This is mark and recapture (the Lincoln-Petersen estimate), first used by C. G. J. Petersen on plaice in 1896.

Numbers checked in code (hypergeometric simulation, 200,000 trials). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_and_recapture

beats.say: Count your fish wrong, and your lake gets fished out.
You can't drain it to count. You need just two fishing trips.
Trip one: catch 200 fish, clip a tiny tag on each, and let them go.
Wait a few days, so they swim back in among the rest.
Trip two: catch 200 again, and count the tagged ones. Say 20.
20 out of 200 is one in 10. So your 200 tagged fish are a tenth of the lake. That's 2,000 fish.
But one trip could be luck. How far off can you be?
Simulate thousands of trips on a computer. Nine trips in 10, you'd say somewhere from 1,500 to 2,900.
Catch 500 each trip, and it tightens to 1,800 to 2,300.
The catch: if tagged fish learn to dodge your net, you count too few, and you'd think the lake holds almost twice the fish.
The share of tagged fish in your net is the share of the lake you tagged. A Danish biologist counted plaice this way in 1896.
So, tag 50 frogs, catch 40, and 8 are tagged. How many frogs?
